title: The Statute of Anne and the Birth of Copyright (1710)
explainer: Before 1710, control over a printed work in England was a trade privilege held by the London Stationers' Company, not a right held by the author. Britain's Statute of Anne introduced the idea that an author holds a time-limited legal right to control copying of a work, after which it enters the public domain — the basic structure that still underlies modern copyright, licensing, and fair-use questions a developer runs into when reusing code or content.

title: Copyleft: Using Copyright Against Itself (1989)
explainer: Richard Stallman's GNU General Public License, first published in 1989, used copyright law's own mechanism to produce the opposite of its usual effect: instead of restricting copying, it legally guarantees that a work and anything built from it stay free to run, study, modify, and redistribute. Recognizing 'copyleft' as a licensing strategy built on top of ordinary copyright — not an absence of legal rights — is the key to reading real open-source licenses (MIT, GPL, Apache) correctly rather than treating them as interchangeable.
